title: Resilient Egress Circuit and Backpressure Playbook for Private Deployments
author: Maya Chen
body:
Overview:

This playbook defines the patterns, configuration examples, operational checks, and escalation steps for building resilient egress circuits and backpressure controls in Redwood private deployments (VPC and on-prem). It applies to both single-tenant and multi-tenant private installs where outbound network and third-party service behavior can affect runtime stability, cost, or customer SLAs. Use this guide when designing tenant egress, service mesh egress policies, or when instrumenting runtime to avoid cascading resource exhaustion.

Goals and scope:
- Limit blast radius from external dependency failures (third-party APIs, cloud provider egress throttles).
- Ensure predictable token consumption and model-serving latency under transient egress failures.
- Provide safe, observable backpressure signals to callers and an operator-friendly recovery path.
- Cover config examples for Envoy, Envoy RateLimit service, service mesh (Istio/Linkerd) and the Redwood egress-proxy component.

When to apply this playbook:
- Any private deploy that routes traffic through customer-managed or provider-managed egress proxies.
- Deploys that have high downstream variability (third-party OCR/TTS providers, remote tokenizers).
- Multi-tenant clusters where noisy egress can starve GPU worker pools.

Key concepts (short):
- Egress circuit: a combination of routing + enforcement components that control outbound flows (egress proxy, rate-limiter, circuit-breaker).
- Backpressure: deliberate slowing or rejecting of requests at the ingress or control-plane when downstream cannot keep up.
- Latency SLOs vs capacity SLOs: we sacrifice soft latency for safety but maintain 99.9% availability of the control-plane.

Architecture patterns:

1) Default architecture (recommended):
- Tenant -> Ingress -> redwood-runtime -> egress-proxy (Envoy) -> external service
- egress-proxy runs per-region; applies per-tenant rate limits, TLS inspection, and routing to isolated upstreams.
- A shared "egress-rls" Redis cluster stores token-bucket state for multi-pod consistency.

ASCII diagram:

[Ingress] -> [redwood-runtime workers (K8s)] -> [egress-proxy (Envoy cluster)] -> [RateLimit service / Circuit state store] -> [External Upstreams]

2) Hardened architecture (recommended for regulated customers):
- Per-tenant egress subnets; per-tenant proxy instances (egress-proxy-tenant-<id>) with BGP route policy to force deterministic path and egress telemetry collection.
- Local synthetic upstreams for controlled failover (local stub service that returns cached or degraded responses).

Configuration and thresholds:

Table: Operational thresholds (suggested defaults for private deploys)

| Metric | Threshold (default) | Action when breached | Owner |
|-------|--------------------:|----------------------|-------|
| Egress request rate per-tenant | 100 req/s | Rate-limit to 100r/s; notify tenant | Runtime team |
| Egress 95p latency to external upstream | 500 ms | Start shed non-critical requests; degrade model variant | SRE |
| Egress error rate (5xx or connection failures) | 1% over 5m | Open circuit for 30s; switch to cached fallback | Runtime team |
| Egress queue depth per worker | 200 requests | Reject new requests with 429; enable adaptive batching | SRE/Runtime |
| Token-bucket refill burst size | 2x sustained rate | Temporary burst allowed; then throttle | Runtime team |

Policy primitives and how they combine:
- Token bucket rate limits (per-tenant and per-route): prevents sustained overuse and provides predictable CPU/GPU load.
- Sliding window error budget (per-upstream): opens a circuit when upstream exceeds error budget.
- Queue-based shedding: limit internal queue depth and fail fast or return synthesized responses.
- Priority routing: separate critical control-plane calls from best-effort analytics calls.

Example Envoy config snippets (rate limit + circuit breaker):

1) Envoy cluster circuit breaker (yaml):

cluster_config:
  name: external-ocr
  circuit_breakers:
    thresholds:
      - priority: DEFAULT
        max_connections: 100
        max_pending_requests: 200
        max_requests: 400
        max_retries: 0

2) Envoy filter: rate limit descriptor (pseudo YAML):

rate_limits:
  - actions:
      - request_headers:
          header_name: x-tenant-id
      - remote_address: {}
  timeout: 20ms

Operational patterns and runbook (step-by-step):

A. Pre-deployment checklist (operator):
1. Confirm egress-proxy versions on all nodes match the pinned release.
2. Verify RateLimit service endpoints (primary + standby) are healthy (200 OK /healthz).
3. Validate BGP or NAT rules for per-tenant subnets using the onboarding test suite.
4. Ensure telemetry is enabled for egress: envoy.access_logs, rate_limit metrics, circuit state metrics.
5. Smoke test against a controlled synthetic upstream.

B. Normal operations and detection:
1. Monitoring: dashboards should show per-tenant egress rate, 95th latency, 5xx rate, and queue depth.
2. Alerts (examples):
   - alert: EgressHighErrorRate
     expr: increase(egress_upstream_5xx_total[5m]) / increase(egress_requests_total[5m]) > 0.01
     for: 2m
   - alert: EgressQueueDepthHigh
     expr: sum(avg_over_time(egress_queue_depth[1m])) by (pod) > 200
     for: 1m
3. If any of the above fire, follow the mitigation steps below.

C. Mitigation flow (automated + operator):
1. Automated: On EgressHighErrorRate (>1% over 5m), the circuit opens for the failing upstream. The runtime routes eligible requests to fallback cached responses or slower model variant.
2. Operator: If the circuit remains open for >5m:
   a. Check upstream health and DNS resolution from egress-proxy pods: curl -v to upstream endpoint.
   b. Check TLS handshake failures: envoy TLS context logs.
   c. If upstream degraded due to external provider, engage network team to confirm egress path and coordinate with the provider.
3. If memory or CPU pressure observed on egress-proxy: scale egress-proxy replicas and increase token-bucket capacity temporarily. Confirm CPU/latency tradeoffs.
4. On egress spikes from a single tenant: apply per-tenant hard limits and open a support ticket with tenant account team.

D. Rolling remediation and rollback steps (for global policy changes):
1. Canary: apply new rate-limit and circuit-breaker config to 1% of tenants via configMap with canary label. Observe for 30m.
2. If no regressions, expand to 25% and observe 1h.
3. If a regression occurs at any step, perform config rollback by reverting the configMap and re-loading into Envoy via xDS.
4. Escalation if rollback fails: run the emergency bypass (described below) to route traffic around egress-proxy to a trusted path.

Emergency bypass (operator cook-book):
- Purpose: temporary path to restore customer-critical traffic when egress proxies are causing outages. Use only with approval from SRE lead and customer-facing account owner.

Steps:
1. Open support ticket and notify stakeholders.
2. Update cluster routing policy to add temporary static route from redwood-runtime to upstream IP (via BGP or node-local NAT).
3. Remove rate-limit descriptor for the affected tenant(s) on the egress-proxy for the duration of the bypass.
4. Monitor for overuse and set a strict timer (max 30 minutes) for the bypass window.
5. Re-enable normal flow and re-deploy validated config.

Observability and metrics (required):
- Required metrics to emit from egress-proxy and runtime: egress_requests_total, egress_requests_success_total, egress_requests_5xx_total, egress_latency_ms_bucket, egress_queue_depth, per-tenant_rate_limited_total, circuit_open_count, rate_limit_decision_latency_ms.
- Traces must include the full request path across redwood-runtime -> egress-proxy -> upstream (trace id propagated via x-request-id).
- Log schema: JSON with fields: timestamp, tenant_id, route, upstream, latency_ms, response_code, decision (allow/limit/circuit_open), request_id.

Testing and validation suites:
- Unit tests for rate-limit logic and token-bucket edge cases.
- Integration test harness: simulate burst patterns (1000x) and long tail errors (upstream 50% 5xx) to validate automatic circuit opening and fallback.
- Load test: replay 24 hours of production traffic in staging filtered by tenant to validate queue behavior and backpressure.

Known operational pitfalls and countermeasures:
- Pitfall: cascading opens when token-bucket refills concurrently across pods.
  Countermeasure: use centralized token-store or strongly-consistent Redis with short TTL and jittered refill windows.
- Pitfall: noisy neighbor due to misconfigured tenant quotas.
  Countermeasure: per-tenant telemetry + billing guardrails + temporary hard caps.
- Pitfall: hidden latency spikes when fallback variant requires cold KV cache warmup.
  Countermeasure: pre-warm fallback caches during maintenance windows and maintain an on-disk microcache for last-successful responses.

Ownership and escalation matrix:
- Primary owner (runtime): Runtime Team (runtime-owners@redwood.com) — responsible for config, deployment, and automated fallback.
- Escalation (SRE): SRE Team pager (oncall-sre) — responsible for scaling, emergency bypass, and BGP/NAT changes.
- Customer-facing escalation: Customer Success -> Account Engineering -> Security for sensitive incidents.

Retention and audit requirements:
- Circuit open/close events and rate-limit decisions must be retained for 90 days in raw logs and 2 years in aggregated metrics for compliance evidence.

Appendix A: Example minimal Redundant RateLimit service (pseudo-config)

# Redis-backed RateLimit: simplified example
redis_host: redistun:6379
namespace: rl_service
shards: 3
max_memory_mb: 1024

Appendix B: Troubleshooting checklist (quick)
1. Are egress-proxy pods Restarting? kubectl get pods -n redwood | grep egress-proxy
2. What is the 95th latency to upstream from envoy stats? curl http://envoy-admin:9901/stats | grep upstream_http_rq_time
3. Is the RateLimit service responsive? curl http://ratelimit.internal:8081/healthz
4. Is the redis token-store under write pressure? redis-cli info memory
